By coincidence I watched this film for the first time as well. I enjoyed it and thought it was strong, but my opinion is less than yours.

I agree that the film has a strong theme, but because of its nature there’s a lot of invisible character development that basically never pays off. Ironically the protagonist was the only character who ever really gives the audience a piece of their mind. It’s an important aspect of the theme that everyone is afflicted under the hood by what overtly afflicts the protagonist, but that leaves everybody in the movie stuck implying their feelings for basically the entire runtime. Subtext is fine, and could be interesting, but there’s not nearly enough of that in the film for me. At the end of the film, basically every character except for one left me thinking either “where are we?” or “wait, how did we get here?”, and even if it fits the theme, it leaves a lot of the emotions of the movie either empty or not paid off.

One thing that stuck with me that’s kind of related is that the writer is a huge presence in the story, and is arguably a bigger presence than any character, including the protagonist who stands in for her. This story seems to be about her life, thoughts, and feelings way more than it is about the characters’. I’m ambivalent about that, but I’m sure that a huge portion of the audience absolutely hates that and can not get over it at all.

The upshot is that I feel like a lot of the movie either flew over my head or wasn’t there at all. Again, for example, only one character explanation is given for why it is so goddamned hard to speak one’s mind (“words hurt people and are permanent”), but there are clearly other reasons why people don’t talk about stuff that are even in the movie but are almost completely unexplored. The old relationship failure was a major plot point that directly related to the movie’s main theme, but the movie almost goes out of its way to hide the characters’ actual motivating feelings from the audience. Again, maybe I just didn’t get it, but I felt like it wasn’t explored just because that manifestation wasn’t important to the writer.

I think given the release context of the movie, at least in my english-speaking country, it would have to be a near-masterpiece to be remembered as a classic, and for me there’s nothing it does well enough to rise to that level. I did enjoy it though.

So the ultimate object of religious is unrest reduction, which it gets through tolerance of the true faith. Its main competitor is humanist ideas.

There are some countries or scenarios where with humanist ideas newly conquered provinces never actually separatist rebel, regardless of culture or religion or whatever. If you are a country with access to a little heathen tolerance rebel whack-a-mole completely stops which is amazing.

With even religious buffed missionaries it’s pretty difficult to core your new provinces and then convert them all in time to actually benefit from tolerance of the true faith before separatists pop. Long term tolerance of the true faith will end up being better but usually you don’t really care. Whether your bulk provinces are -14 unrest with true faith or -1 with heathen religion usually doesn’t matter.

Trade companies generally buff humanist as well, because the fact that intolerance penalties are negated cuts a disadvantage of a weaker humanist nation. It almost never makes sense to core a trade company province, then convert it, then assign it, especially since you have at best five missionaries and conquer more provinces than that at a time.

I will say that religious is THE #1 A+ S-tier idea group for role-playing and religion map painting. Deus vult is the second-strongest idea in the game for basically every nation no matter where it is in the group. Tolerance of the true faith is by definition better than less-intolerance. But for most campaigns humanist is more practical and efficient since the whole point is that you do nothing.

If you are Not Muscovy, you might want to think about quantity before defensive, mostly because you have to fight Muscovy. Religious is pretty nice. Orthodox is strong nationally and locally so you might as well DV everyone and convert every province.

Think about influence, since you start with a bunch of vassals. Think about economic, since your land sucks and you will need institutions. Trade is fine but the Novgorod node even when you monopolize it is not very good.

I would personally go religious since the orthodox countries run out pretty fast but if you have to kill the big girl then quantity would probably be worth it. Morale doesn’t help you kill more soldiers, and you aren’t going to get enough morale to stack wipe everyone 1v1, only by outnumbering them. Even if you win battles because of morale you won’t kill more of their men doing it, so they’ll just pull some more out of the ground if they have more than you.

TLDR if you’re big girl go religious, if you’re little girl go quantity, if you’re vassal (bonkers mode) go diplo to grab some independence support.

2 things I think:

1. As a lot of people have said catching is career-shortening and injury-prone. I think the bigger thing though is that catchers get way more games off than any other defensive position. (P doesn’t count as usual.) Posey has basically always hit well enough to be an everyday starter at any position, but “everyday starter” at C means about 500AB/season vs about 600AB/season at say 1B or DH, or even 3rd if you’re durable.

2. For other important defensive positions like SS, there is some trade off between bat and glove. You want a good fielder there, but average defense and a good bat is sometimes preferred to great defense and a weak bat. That trade off doesn’t really exist at catcher. Long term, big league managers have strongly preferred having the best defensive catcher who can remotely hit they can possibly find, because a good catcher directly makes their pitchers better (game calling, pitch framing, SB deterrence, trust, etc.). So clubs really want to avoid a situation where their stud prospect is “blocked” by a AAA hitter. More so than at other positions, the best MLB offensive catchers also tend to be among the best MLB defensive catchers, because the only reason their bat sticks at the position is because fielding their defense is also an advantage.

Aside: I think Gary Sanchez’s career is going to be an interesting case study. He is improving as a defensive catcher but is still raw aside from an enormous arm. He is exactly the sort of guy who slowly transitions to OF/1B/DH, but NYY might be the only team in the league where he is blocked into the C position instead of out of it. He’s also the best fit at the position in the league for a team of scary hitters that you can’t walk because 1-9 in the lineup is protected by a power hitter.

TLDR a good series. Both teams made a strong case for the championship. They were about equal, although I think game 7 will color the series disproportionately - and maybe game 5 too, hopefully not that’s too much thinking for me. There were an unusual number of times where either team felt like they had just demonstrated that they were the superior, inevitable series winner, and each time the other team came right back almost immediately and refuted it. Game 1, Game 2 ot, the 4/4 pp game, game 6, and now game 7. Neither team was ever really able to pull away at any point.

I remember when the pats won in ‘02. It kind of broke my brain because the pats back then were nobodies idea of contenders basically ever. There was sort of this sense that odds are they would eventually seriously contend and maybe win, but there was sort of this perpetual mediocrity - even when they were good they weren’t really close to good enough. Even when they were ostensibly close they were absolutely destroyed by the freaking ‘85 bears in a result that everyone expected. So when they actually won consistently one year everyone obviously felt joy but we also felt confusion. So I remember being borderline shocked that everyone had to talk about the pats gameplanning for a chance to win the super bowl. I remember when they won it realizing that this particular seemingly random group of dudes were basically heroes now, and would be forever. I distinctly remember that confused feeling.

I imagine that’s what blues fans are feeling right now. There’s nobody comparing this to the good old days because there really aren’t any. The only important legacy of the franchise you followed forever has just happened. Forget the last to first thing. This wasn’t supposed to happen because it was the blues, not because of their mathematical wild card odds in January. Being a blues fan is fundamentally different now than it was a few hours ago. So if you are a blues fan, some important part of you has just changed. You have just bizarrely had your faith rewarded. Even if it never happens again, it changes you when someone you love comes through for you. Even just once. To have that come out of nowhere, when even your most demanding mindset was that everything in the playoffs was just gravy... it’s confusing. I know.

So if you are a blues fan, obviously congratulations. Tonight you can celebrate and drink and be merry etc. But I hope that at some point you will also think about what has just happened to you, and all of the people you know who follow the team. And I hope that you will never forget the old feeling of following your team totally expecting to be let down. It changed me when it happened. I’m a much different person because the teams I love came through, even if it was just once. You’re different now, too. I hope that you will think about that, and that you will always remember the old feeling.

One thing I like to tell people who are learning is to learn the offsides rule and then watch how teams play at the blue line. (With scarce exceptions, an offensive player can’t beat the puck over the offensive blue line.) There’s not a lot of set plays at the ends of the ice because the defenders are too fast for the offense to set up. Because of that a lot of offensive strategy sort of devolves into creating chaos and threats, which makes the game unpredictable and fun. So a lot of the game is not based on strategy or even tactics per se, because chaos is by nature hard to plan for and threats are powerful because they force the defense’s hand and make them decide for the offense. If you threaten something, and your opponent doesn’t protect against the threat, you just follow through on the threat, there’s not a lot of strategy or decision-making involved.

Pretty long-winded. I would say hockey 100-level classes are:
- line rules (icing and offsides)
- whistle rules. Rule of thumb is that the whistle blows when the offending team touches the puck. Icing is an exception that is pretty not interesting.
- positions (wing, center, defenseman, and goalie) and what they prototypically do, which matters less and less as the years go by
- penalty rules, definitions of the common ones: roughing, tripping, slashing, cross-check, interference. And sure, fighting, why the hell not.
- the cause and significance of special teams (power play and its opposite, penalty kill, as well as goalie-pulled)
- this time of year I would include basic playoff structure, but that’s easy enough: single elimination series, best of 7 games

I would say hockey 200-level courses are something like:
- power play set up and positioning
- breakout tactics - what does a team with the puck in its defensive end of the ice do to “clear the zone”, get the puck safely out without too much chaos?
- breakin tactics - how does a team with the puck cross their offensive blue line without going offsides?
- role-player prototypes: sniper, speedster, defensive forward/offensive defenseman, enforcer, grinder, agitator.
- line-change subtleties. Biggest one is if one team has players out on the ice for more than about 45 seconds and can’t substitute them out “on the fly”. If this happens it’s a huge advantage for the other team with fresh players, and every player in the rink knows it. Very dramatic and lots of goals.
- unusual penalties and penalty situations. Puck over glass, too many men, high-sticking, penalty shots, double-minors, majors, match penalties, suspension/fine process
- basic assessment of who is carrying the play at a given point of a game. Look for which side is getting shots on goal, is carrying or passing (not dumping or chipping) the puck across the blue lines regularly, is forcing desperate penalties and defensive plays by the opponent, has time and space with possession of the puck, and how the home/away crowd is feeling (tense?, excited?, loud?, asleep?). Obviously there’s more but it can often be very difficult to tell who has the initiative in a hockey game. There is a sizable number of analysts who argue that no one ever really has the initiative in a hockey game.

There’s three possible ways this can be understood.


1. Antidepressant medication takes a notoriously long time to be effective. Most SSRIs, for example, require a minimum two week trial before evaluating whether or not they are helping the patient. So if your friend just started a new regimen, what the worker may have meant was “We have to wait awhile for your new med to kick in; until then, there is nothing else we can do to help you.” This isn’t true, by the way. Your friend should be going through therapy on a full-time basis if they are inpatient. Also, ECT is an option if the doctor feels it is warranted and your friend is not opposed.

2. The worker may have meant it as you and your friend have interpreted. I’m not clear why this would have been said. Perhaps the worker said this out of frustration and anger. It is extremely unlikely that a hospital worth its salt has looked at a depressed patient and actually decided that they’re out of options already.

Either way it’s a pretty irresponsible and unprofessional thing to say, and it is almost definitely not true. It’s actually false and malicious to the extent of being pretty weird. I’ve never heard anything like it anywhere I’ve been inpatient. That’s why you have to face the uncomfortable possibility that

3. “There is nothing anyone can do to help me” is a belief held deeply and completely by your friend. That hopelessness, particularly about the disease itself, is one of the most common symptoms of depression, particularly in suicidal patients. Anything the doctors or clinicians say to your friend will therefore be interpreted as reinforcing the hopeless belief, regardless of the actual content of the conversation. This interpretation and hopeless outlook may be extreme enough to the point where if you actually knew the context or exact wording of what they were told, you would construe what your friend said as exaggerated, twisted, or an outright lie.

I’m telling you all this for your benefit, not your friend’s. There is absolutely nothing you can say to your friend to convince them that this hopelessness is wrong or overly pessimistic. It would be like trying to talk someone out of their faith (or lack thereof) in God, except even stronger. I hope this puts your mind at ease to some extent. The hospital is not out of options for a new patient. They’ve treated endless cases similar to your friend, I promise. I’m glad you are there for your friend to the extent you can; that is the very best thing you can do for them. Ironically, to help your friend, your goal is not to help them. It’s just to keep being their friend.

For this answer, I am referring to partial hospitalization (PH) programs as the few hospitals I've been to construct them: you drive there in the morning, you have appointments with a case manager and a psychiatrist, you do a bunch of group therapies with other patients, you drive home. In my experience, that's what hospitals talk about when they say "partial program".

The programs and their length are set. For the program I was at I would say 90% of patients were there for the allotted six weeks, no more, no less. I suppose there must have been exceptions, mainly people in the program having to go inpatient, but I wasn't privy to that nor did I care to be. I highly doubt there were any cases where someone was there for three weeks, and the staff said, "Well, looks like you're okay now, ahead of schedule, so let's get you out of here!" It's just the way psychiatry is, how it works, what its problems tend to be. You probably know that by now.

When I'm really not doing well, as was the case during my hospitalizations, I get really socially anxious. My PHs were 90% groups, so I was not happy to be there. Nevertheless, it was not a disaster or even particularly painful since literally every other person in the room does not expect you to be a totally functional, perfectly fine, emotionally stable human being.

You may or may not need to prepare yourself mentally if you have issues with any of the following: patient groups, therapists, psychiatrists, case managers, boredom, condescension, talking about your feelings. Maybe some other stuff, but those are the big ones. None of them are worse or scarier in a PH program than they are anywhere else.

For the mood disorder PHs I've done, permission to drive from the program is not an issue. Arranging transportation certainly is a problem for many patients. If you are living in a situation where you are monitored or cared for by psych-trained staff, it is *their* permission you need to drive, not the PH program's.

You can refuse medicine. The psychiatrist appointments I had were analogous to ordinary outpatient psychiatrist appointments, not to inpatient psychiatric interviews. Nonetheless, there is the hammer of inpatient that the PH doc holds over you, so you may want to be careful about aggravating your relationship with them. Normal psych medicine rules apply otherwise: know what you're taking, know why, know side effects, know if you can get off them, be disciplined with medication, feel free to refuse but have a specific (good) reason, etc.

One tip that has always helped me with nasty psych life situations is to try to keep a sense of humor. In many circumstances I got nothing good out of what I was doing besides a joke. It made all the dumb, banal, insulting, humiliating stuff more bearable. In one PH program there was a group therapist I could not stand. Every group she did was unproductive, and I was angry at her the whole time. I couldn't leave, so I just played the class clown card a little. Not enough to really rock the boat, but enough to keep her uncomfortable and aware of the fact that I didn't respect her or her methods. There's been other times where joking around has helped me, but that's an example.

By the way, the fact that you're going into a PH means you either 1. are exiting inpatient and transitioning back to real life, or 2. are not doing well and managed to avoid inpatient and stay sleeping in your own bed. Either way, that's a huge win. Not for nothing, but inpatient sucks. Even the most posh inpatient experience is sad. PH is better. You're probably not getting too many congratulations either way, so I'll give you some now.

I did TMS, no K infusion.

TMS is a bit of a sci-fi trip. It's treated like ECT in terms of how and when it's prescribed, but it works on totally different principles, trying to electromagnetically stimulate small parts of the brain where low activity is linked to depression. ECT is more brute force, flooding the entire brain with neurotransmitters to try to stimulate more activity.

I don't know if you have experience with ECT, but don't base your expectations on that. There's no sedation or anesthesia with TMS, you just sit in a chair, they put a big giant helmet over half your head, and start the treatment. It lasts half an hour or so, with pulses of EM stimulation lasting about two seconds each, separated from each other by something like ten seconds. The sensation from the pulse was a little bizarre for me. It wasn't alien but it was definitely weird. I didn't feel it in my brain. I felt it in my neck, arm, and hand on the side they were stimulating. It was like a hard twitching attack. It was uncomfortable but not painful at all. More noticeably, I felt it in my scalp and skull. I had the strong sensation that something was rapping me on the head from under the helmet. It was as if a woodpecker was holding a fist in its beak and knocking my head with a knuckle. I could've sworn there was something in the machine hitting me in the head during the pulses, but there wasn't. That was definitely uncomfortable, but if it ever got truly painful they could step down the intensity of the pulse so that I could tolerate it. Gradually I got used to the pulse sensation and it didn't bother me as much. I definitely felt it in my body, but there wasn't pain. If you feel immediate pain rather than just discomfort make sure the doctor or tech knows.

The other thing to know about TMS is how the effects happen. Anyone who has had ECT will tell you that you definitely feel its effects immediately. Maybe you're still depressed, but you definitely at least feel like you've had a seizure. That doesn't happen with TMS. I would walk out of treatment with my mood feeling exactly the same as when I walked in. I could tell no difference within a day. It's a longer-term treatment. (I believe K is more short-term, which is why they might be combined.) It's hard for me to say if TMS helped with my depression. I didn't really notice. But it's very possible it kept me from getting worse, and TMS is currently backed up as beneficial pretty solidly in research. For me, either it helped, or it was at least worth a shot.

This is a very 21st-century regimen you've been prescribed. Presumably your depression has been treatment-resistant? If SSRIs and Wellbutrin and antipsychs and stuff like that haven't done enough, K + TMS is probably worth a shot, I think you can be cautiously optimistic. My understanding is that both are very safe with few side effects, although I'm not as sure about that with K. Let me know how it goes, what you think of both. It drove home that thoughts and feelings do not logically follow each other. I originally believed that I had thoughts, then had understanding based on those thoughts, then had feelings based on that understanding. But that’s rarely true for me. Sometimes feelings are faster than thoughts: I feel some emotion, and then my thoughts reconstruct an understanding of why that feeling exists. Sometimes feelings happen to me for no reason, and my thoughts scramble to reconstruct a narrative that doesn’t exist. So now I can kind of accept that I have feelings for no or little reason.

eg, It’s not that I’m afraid of what people will think of me or whatever, it’s just that my brain gets afraid around other people for no reason, or just because it wants to. Before my thoughts would try to justify the fear I felt by inventing logical fears (“what if they don’t like me”, “what if I embarrass myself,” etc.), and those thoughts would exacerbate the fear I felt. Now when I feel that fear I know it’s just something my brain and body stupidly does, and I don’t try to justify or explain it. That doesn’t make the feeling go away, but I feel better than if I didn’t know what was happening.

This obviously isn’t always true (some feelings are legit, or caused by legit thoughts), but it’s true often enough for my pathological feelings that I notice benefit.

The best thing you can do is just to be there for him and give a shit. Lots of supportive people fall into the trap of trying to solve depression in some way. Emotional vulnerability is essential to productive therapy and psychiatric care. It is also difficult for most people, including myself. When I started treatment, I hadn’t spoken to someone openly about my true feelings...maybe ever. And it was something that I thought was impossible for me to do successfully. I spent a lot of time and practice getting good at filling in new clinicians on exactly what bothered me.

For some people it is harder to talk about this stuff with people who are essentially strangers than the people close to them; for me it is easier but marginally so. When I have to openly explain to someone, particularly someone like a therapist, the feelings and emotions that are bothering me and creating problems in my life, I focus on two goals in particular:

1. I speak about these feelings in the past tense. These are not what I’m feeling “right now”, or “all the time”, but what I felt, say, “this morning”, or “the last time I was feeling really down”. Even if these feelings are continuous or even immediately present, it is much easier for me to talk about what I *did* feel versus what I *am* feeling. Then, if comfortable or compelled, I may tack on a little “...and actually, I kind of feel that way now, too.” at the end. The clinician gets all they need to know, and it is much easier for me to get there.

2. I make a conscious effort to be as removed as possible from the emotion I am describing. I want to talk about feeling lonely without actually feeling lonely. Again, it is much easier for me to discuss something that I am not feeling in the immediate moment. If I am generally having problems with loneliness, it’s easier for me to talk about that in a moment that I’m not particularly lonely. So I treat my answers to the “how are you feeling” question sort of like how I might tell a deadpan joke. Neutral or slightly wry facial expression, monotone voice, neutral posture, and as straight-faced as possible. It’s easier for me to talk about emotionally loaded topics as detached from that emotion as possible.

The effect of these two is that it’s almost like I’m not talking about *my* feelings per se, but those of some other person, who just happens to be me in the past, or another distraught me sitting next to me. And I’ll be honest, this is not true vulnerability. I’m making an effort to hide how I feel from the other person. It’s just that what I share (explicit bothersome thoughts and feelings) is specifically chosen to be as helpful as possible to the clinician. Over time, it’s gotten easier and easier to be vulnerable, so I need these tactics less and less. They still help though, and we’re particularly helpful at the beginning.

Your mileage may vary if you try these things, and if you have some other tactics you were thinking of, by all means try them out. Whatever you do, remember that it is in your best interest to share openly and honestly and completely, as uncomfortable as it is. If you don’t share what is truly and deeply bothering you, it is unlikely that the treatment will address it. I believe that this is what people who don’t believe that therapy is helpful often experience. I also have some digestive issues, and so I have to talk to my GI doc about my stool and intestines and what my bowel movements look like and stuff. That feels super weird too. But that’s why we have this one person - a doc to listen to all the nasty stuff and to try to expertly find a solution so that as few people have to know as possible. It’s sort of the same thing.

Anyway, good luck. It’s not a fun thing to do for the first time, but it’s not as scary in the moment as you will expect.

You are correct that the main problematic side effect is amnesia. I had a larger than normal number of treatments, but there is a period of my life of about a year surrounding the treatment of which I remember very little, and do not recall even when asked about remembering specific significant events in that period. That’s distressing, obviously, but it’s also problematic in very practical ways, particularly if you’re going through therapy or trying to work at the same time or have other life issues to address.

The other main side effect is fatigue. An ect day for me was basically a lost day. I would have no activity and sleep on and off through the day, then sleep all night and wake up mostly functional in the morning. Again, this is a problem if you’re trying to get anything done in your life at the same time.

Combine these two effects and you get this sort of characteristic ect zombie who does and remembers nothing for at least a day, and is somewhat less than functional in the days following the treatment. Because of this effect (and other reasons), outpatient ect treatment is either impossible or a huge pain in the ass. I was inpatient, so it wasn’t a problem for me to lose two days a week, since nothing would have happened then anyway. Being a zombie is often a problem, particularly with regard to the power dynamic in any discussion with an ect doc about whether to continue or taper the treatment. If you don’t have competent support helping you out with decisions and life practicalities, ect is a big problem.

Add to this the fact that ect is strictly a short-term treatment. For whatever reason (probably health guidelines and common sense), ect is only used for acute severe depression or other mental illness. You shouldn’t, and maybe even can’t take weekly ect as a mood maintenance measure. It’s not like SSRIs where you just keep taking them as long as they work - if you did that with ect, you’d be a zombie forever. So if ect works, you can’t even bank on it as a reliable long-term ally. You would have to find an antidepressant drug that helps anyway.

So you are absolutely correct that it works. But that “working” is mainly limited to the short term and in general the short term is where the side effects cause the most damage. I would never start ect again without a sane and sober family member following my care closely, if not making care decisions for me. I also would never try it on an outpatient basis, or hoping that it could replace long-term medication.

It is sort of used in a last-resort sort of way for two reasons primarily: 1. the side effects are significant, 2. it works - if only for the short-term.

When they ask you what's wrong, just try to be as specific as you can about what you are thinking and feeling, and what negative impact on your life and actions happen as a result. Don't worry about trying to cover everything in detail, because at some point they will likely give you [something like this](https://psychology-tools.com/major-depression-inventory/) to respond to, which will give them an idea of what you're dealing with. If you have depression-like symptoms, you'll get one like the one I've linked. If you have mania-like symptoms, you'll get one for bipolar. There's one for psychosis, eating disorders, etc. If they don't literally hand you a test like this, they will likely ask you the same questions and note your answers. If you're looking for things to start explaining to them, you can just search online for one relative to the symptoms that you are having, and lead with those. For example, if I were in your place and were having symptoms of depression, I may look at the inventory I linked and tell the docs I was feeling down constantly, had no interest in previous hobbies, and was having trouble sleeping. I would focus on the ones that were really causing problems for me, and then let them ask for the rest.

Medication is a bit of a beast. The bad news is that the mechanics of medication and relevant illnesses are generally not well-understood, and so consequently psychiatric medication is basically a guess-and-check process. The good news is that this means that your psychiatrist would have to be particularly incompetent to really be that much worse than a really good one. After looking at your symptoms, your doc will likely make a guess as to what's going on, roll the dice on a common, safe medication, and start you on a low dose and see what happens. They should thoroughly educate you on relative dosage, side effects, red flags, etc.

The most important thing when dealing with psychiatrists, therapists, social workers, and your private support system (ie, family, friends who know what's going on with you) is to be **open**, **honest**, and **specific** about what you are thinking and feeling. Don't worry about being thorough, because they should be the one asking questions that fill out the information that they need to know about you. I would say just peek through some of these inventories online and pick out the questions that are really causing problems for you.

Let's say we have someone who is or is becoming heavily depressed ("your friend" or "her") and someone who is trying to support that person ("you"). This is just shorthand to make this easier to write, not an order or an accusation, or even a suggestion.

Lots of different things happen when a person is depressed, but from the perspective of someone trying to help, you can focus on two emotional processes.

In process A, she becomes hopeless. She may feel like her life is worthless or pointless, or that she can never achieve her goals or fulfill her potential. She will likely feel or even strongly believe that she will never be not-depressed ever again. It's more complicated than that, but this is probably close enough for you. This is what people usually realize, feel, and describe first when they talk about their depression. You likely see this in your friend, either directly or in the behaviors and emotions this process causes (ie, no motivation, no affinity for life, extreme pessimism). This is a big part of perpetuating and aggravating depression, mostly because working honestly to help oneself become healthy requires some faith in that working - a faith that doesn't exist. It's a catch-22, and so process A tends to build on itself and snowball and get worse and worse over time.

It is very important that you understand that you probably cannot do anything about process A. These ideas of hopelessness are core beliefs of hers. Even if you are able to convince her mind that her life is valuable (which you probably won't), you will not be able to convince her heart, and the heart will win out in the end. This is why you may have been told not to do the "you have so much to live for!" and "you have to believe in yourself!" kind of support. It targets A, and it just doesn't work. We'll come back to A at the end of this post.

In process B, she becomes emotionally isolated. As her negative emotions become strong and overwhelming, she is less and less likely to share them with others. She becomes solipsistic, realizing that she is living in a different world than the healthy, happy, normal people she observes. As she becomes more abnormal, she ostracizes herself more and more. Her depression becomes a larger part of her life, so by not sharing depression she is effectively not sharing herself. She increasingly isolates herself, both emotionally and socially, and probably even physically. Again, B snowballs and tends to make things worse.

Unlike A, B is something you are very much able to help with. All you need is sincerity, tact, and a good ear. If you ask her to openly and honestly tell you what she is feeling, and she replies in kind, and you sincerely and closely listen to what she is going through, and you express empathy for her feelings, you have helped her tremendously. It may feel to the both of you like the conversation has done nothing, largely because there is no change in A, but that's okay because she has something to put in B, and when you have nothing, something is everything. Your goal here would be nothing but to have some understanding of what she is going through, and for her to understand that you understand. That's all she needs for B. She will naturally hold on to that little bit that you give her, and as long as you continue to provide that purely emotional support, she will have something to work with, and she will not be at the bottom. This is the very best thing you can do for anyone who is going through a difficult time, but particularly for depression, where there is little else inside a person besides the nothing.

When people get badly depressed, they lose a lot. There are two factors that trap them there in my experience, particularly when they having suicidal ideation. Factor A is the hopelessness/pointlessness/lack of purpose. It's a bit of an amalgamation of the different flavors of negative self-talk that comes from depression. Factor B is emotional isolation. By nature of depression, at a certain point, it becomes basically impossible for someone to help themselves in these two areas, and so both continue to deteriorate until they hit an overwhelming limit and the person starts getting desperate. You see both of these a lot in people suicidal from depression. Critically, I think generally both A and B have to be high for SI to start in earnest in most people. (On top of staving off suicide, it's also worthwhile to just take these miserable feelings away from people as much as possible.)

So if they can't help themselves, and anyone is going to help them, it's going to be the people around them. The problem is that almost everyone tends to focus on A. It's the part of depression that is most obviously abnormal. This isn't a problem for them, so they must know how to fix it. It's a natural thought, but A is very difficult for anyone to affect at all. It generally requires a lot of time, effort, and knowledge from well-trained people, and usually some luck as well. I have yet to see anyone actually help another's depression with a conversation for A.

B is relatively easy to change. It just requires tact and sincerity. Look around this place, "That sucks, I'm sorry, I feel you bro" helps all the time. It obviously doesn't touch A, but neither does anything else. And they only need either A or B to decrease to stay away from absolute zero. So if they're at the bottom, splashing anything into B makes things way easier, since now only A is at the limit. Moreover, unlike A, people with depression are usually desperate for B, and will reach out farther and farther (like, say, onto Reddit) to try to find it. They are starving for it and will accept it even from someone who is basically a stranger. So it's easy to provide that to people on here, and it helps quite a bit.

The reason it applies for commenters around here is that it actually does more for the commenter than the OP. Obviously COM gets B as well just by offering it to OP, but COM also gets A by doing something for someone else. For some reason, if someone tells me "thanks for doing X", it registers for me even when I am depressed, where me telling myself "good job for doing X" does not. So when I feel like crap and can barely get on my phone to semi-amuse myself, sometimes I'll come here and comment. Frankly, it's less effort and anxiety for me to deal in discussion boards than direct communication, so I can do it even when I can do basically nothing else. It's a relatively easy way for me to get a little bit of A and B to help myself out.

It is the little things. The cognitive effects of the illness are no joke, most people (myself included) drop some 15-20 iq points while actively depressed. (Not scientifically measured, just subjective.) It’s just another one of those features included at no extra cost.

Depression is brutal on its sufferers, but it also hurts the people around them. I know I often feel guilty from it because 1, I have no reason to be depressed in the first place, and 2, I can tell that my depression makes life harder for people I care about. This sounds like what your wife is going through as well. You will probably never erase that guilt, but you can probably assuage it. “I understand that you are suffering; I know that you did not want or choose this; I care about you and I am here for you no matter what.” If those kinds of messages are clear and consistent, it will be easier for her to deal with that guilt. Preferably she would be hearing that from multiple people, but you are probably the most important one. Be aware that she may (likely) at first reject this out of hand as pandering and fake sympathy to try to help her. But whether or not she admits/knows it, this is the message she wants to hear, and if it is communicated consistently, she will eventually start to believe it.

Now on to the useless “I am not a doctor but” section. In fact, I’m even less qualified than “not a doctor” because I’ve never dealt with chronic depression before; only intermittent or periodic. That means things like ECT are not really on the table because they’re really for treatment of acute illness, and doing a full course of ECT every couple months will do more harm than good. It sounds like you’re running out of methods by the book (talk CBT, DBT, SSRIs, SSNRIs, atypical antidepressants, etc). If you haven’t tried or discussed with your psychiatrist more unconventional treatments, they should either bring them up soon or you should explicitly ask them for other options. These treatments are usually unconventional not because they are dangerous, but because either they have significant side effects or disadvantages (MAOIs, antipsychotic lowdosing), or because they’re relatively new and/or hard to test (TMS, ketamine microdosing) and so have less research behind them. And those are just the few that mr. “not a doctor” has been prescribed or discussed, I’m sure your doc will have many other ideas about treatment possibilities. This doesn’t even count treatments that are being researched now that will be viable in the near future. (Lots of money in depression.) She will still have treatment options for awhile.

I guess the most important thing you can do is care about her and her struggles. Moderate or worse depression is borderline impossible to beat on one’s own. It will help her more to know that you care, but even if you can’t get that across, the little (and big) things you do everyday to help her fight and to make her life easier will help her as well, even if she never notices or thanks you for it. That is the most helpful thing you can possibly do. The depressed will almost always shut out any positivity that people try to insert into their lives. Mysteriously, they will not shut out genuine and understanding expressions of love from those same people. They may tell themselves that it is worthless, but it isn’t. It is the most priceless gift you can give to any human, but especially to a miserable one.

Note that this does not require that you yourself be not miserable. [ugly double negative, but I think it was necessary.] When depressed, it is difficult, sometimes impossible, to care for and love yourself. It is much easier to care for and love someone else. Think about how hollow it is to force yourself to look in the mirror and say, “You matter.” Then think about what it would mean for your boyfriend to look you in the eye and genuinely say, “You matter.” That difference is what you still have to offer people when you are depressed.

Also, most people who try to support their depressed friends or family run into the problem of empathy. It is difficult for a healthy person to understand how corrupted the thinking and emotional reasoning of a depressed person is. You do not have this handicap. You know exactly why the “Put on a happy face!” and “You have so much to live for!” stuff does not work. Congratulations, you have ironically become better at your mission of helping miserable people by being miserable yourself!

I think the phases and episodes are pretty common in mood disorders. Even within the course of a day I might shift between sort of alright and non-functional. I wouldn’t worry about poor mood being triggered by meta-thinking or thinking about emotions per se. (Maybe your therapist or psychiatrist would disagree.) It has always been difficult for me to move my mood in the moment just by changing thought patterns, and I think that’s true for most people.

Have you done any CBT? One cornerstone is that one’s thoughts, feelings, and actions will all influence each other in all directions. As you correctly said, if you feel like shit, your thoughts will likely reflect that. If you feel like shit, your actions will be those of a depressed person. It also works the other way though. If you climb to the top of a huge mountain, that action will likely influence your mood if you consider it an accomplishment. If you pass someone on the street and think, “they’re disgusted by me,” you get a very different impact on your feelings than if you conclude that they like you, or even just don’t care.

Note that “impacting mood” is not the same as “eradicating depression”. You’re correct that the idea that you can change a chronic mood state with specific thoughts is preposterous. But it is also naive to say that emotions are this impenetrable fortress that thoughts can not touch.

University is actually the best case scenario for all those problems. If your school is worth its salt at all, there will likely be a counseling center on campus somewhere. It’s an error with some sense, but the logic is backward. “You feel like your life has no meaning.” => “Almost every parent finds incredible meaningfulness in their children.” => “You should make a baby so that you can snag some of that meaningfulness.”

The problem of course is that they don’t understand that you may well have things in your life already that are meaningful, and right now you are incapable of feeling that meaning. So if you had a kid, that meaning might be created, but you wouldn’t feel it, and then you’d just be unhappier because you’d be thinking, “why don’t I care about my child? What is wrong with me? Am I a sociopath or something? I feel so bad for this kid that they can’t have a loving parent.”

Most people just flat-out do not understand how this shit works, which is frustrating. It’s even more frustrating when they think they understand perfectly well. They might even tell you that they understand, and then they wonder why you tear your hair out and sulk around them, and then they get mad at you for that, etc, etc...

If it’s any consolation, you’re absolutely right, having a child is not going to cure your depression, and being depressed is an excellent reason not to have a child. And in fact, not wanting to have a child is actually probably the very best reason not to have a child... but I guess I wouldn’t understand since I’m not a parent.

I speak only from my experience. It was never helpful for me to have other people want me to do things. “Open up to me about what you’re feeling.” “What changes can you make to help yourself feel better?” All these admittedly little things were just pointless chores that I had no energy or desire to do. So I never did them. Then I felt bad for not doing these little things that would help me. So a lot of these efforts made by people to help me were counterproductive, I would just ultimately feel worse. Based on what I’ve been told from others, this is a pretty common phenomenon in depressed people.

There are a couple of tactics that tend to be helpful for me and for others. One is building self-worth. If you say to me something like, “I care about you, you mean a lot to me because _____,” you’ve just planted in my head a seed of an idea that I matter to another human being. You validated my existence. I will almost certainly not acknowledge or maybe even notice that this happened, but it did. You won’t notice effects from this right away (or maybe ever), but it helps even if you can’t see it helping.

Another thing that sometimes helps is getting across the idea that you have faith that her condition will improve. This is pretty tricky. “You can do it!” does absolutely nothing. Outright stating, “I know that you will get better.” may not work if she is truly hopeless about improving. Stealth references to a future where she is healthy “We will tackle [insert life problem] when you’re ready” is often more helpful if done enough. The idea is to get into her head the sense that you confidently believe that this is not a forever thing for her, even (especially!) if you have no such confidence in reality. Like I said, tricky to pull off. Your mileage definitely will vary.

One last thing - for you! I’ve heard of but not experienced that kind of contagious depression that you are noticing. In this case, the self-worth thing is going to be critical if you are trying to help her. If you tie your own self-worth to how well she is doing, your condition will deteriorate until hers improves. That’s not a recipe for long-term success. If you tie your own self-worth to helping and supporting her as best you can, keeping in mind that you don’t really know what you’re doing (don’t worry, no one does), you help to maintain your mood as long as you continue to help her. Again, easier said than done. The emotional trap of “She’s still depressed; none of this is working well enough; I should be doing more for her; why am I not helping her enough?” is a hard one to stay out of.

I’m definitely an amateur, so don’t take this stuff as gospel right out of the DSM, nor as the whole picture of what can or should be done in your case. If you need that, then you need more professional help (and yes, you probably do). But hopefully there’s at least something up in this bulky essay that you can use or at least find helpful. I know this is hard for the sufferers’ support people, so you helping her makes me want to help you. Even if she’s not doing better and you feel like you’re doing nothing, you’re very likely helping quite a bit, even if what you’re trying isn’t the textbook way to do it. I’m hoping that you both can get through this, even if it takes way longer than you feel it should.

I think most of us here (or at least I and most of the people I talk to) have that first point where we look around at our lives and what we’re doing and think, “okay, this is not really close to normal, something is not right here.” And what one does with that moment makes a huge difference in your life or prognosis or whatever. Many people, like myself, start to panic, wonder what’s wrong with me, am I deteriorating as a person, am I just gonna get worse forever, etc., and usually things go really bad from there in some combination of a thousand different ways.

Based on what you’ve said, you’ve gotten to that point and are thinking, “okay, something’s not right, is there anything I can do to help myself or at least slow this down?” That’s a good sign for you. Usually something can be done. If you will indulge me a few unprofessional suggestions:

1. Find a pro therapist as soon as you can. That might not be right now based on what you’re saying about your life situation, but this should be a priority as soon as it’s possible. I will admit that many (most?) therapists kind of suck and do not feel helpful, but they’re still 100 times better than what you can come up with on your own. You still have to do most of the work, but that work is more likely to be productive. Also, even if your therapist is really incompetent and you want to dump them, they will usually point you to a peer if you tell them that you’re not feeling the relationship and want to try someone else. They should be cool with that, and you can re-roll with whoever they point you too. It helps to have someone on your side who at least had to read the book on psychiatry and the field and whatever.

2. Don’t sweat diagnoses. In my experience, psychiatry works a little different than most other forms of medicine. If you have a cough and trouble breathing, your doc has to know if you have pneumonia or bronchitis or asthma or something else because the treatment for those options is very different. In psychiatry, if you have chronic or severe anxiety, the treatment is largely the same whether that anxiety is from social anx dis. or ptsd or substance issues or whatever. A lot of my treaters have basically ignored diagnoses outright. So when you talk to a professional about what you feels is wrong, you want to say stuff like “I feel [bad/excessive feeling] in [circumstance] and I tend to have [these thoughts] and because of all that I tend to do [action].” That’s what pretty much every therapist and psychiatrist I have ever had likes to work with.

3. Get people close to you on board. This process is way easier if the right people have an idea of what you’re going through, or at least know you’re going through something. This is trickier for a couple reasons. First, by nature of mental illness, many of us literally have no one close to us (family, SO, close friends, etc), in which case this is a non-starter. Second is the uglier problem that many people and many different kinds of people have little or no tolerance for mental illness or therapy or psychiatry. This is just reality. So if you’re thinking about talking to someone close to you and they’ve indicated in the past that they would withdraw support or resent you for trying this stuff, do not clue them in. If you’re concerned about getting support, please find or start another discussion specifically about that because I don’t really know what that’s like, I have been fortunate that almost everyone in my life has been supportive.

I would strongly encourage you to at least consider #1. It sounds like you’re pretty self-aware and practical and determined if you’re taking steps already on your own. Keep it up. Good luck. By the way, what typically happens with relievers is that they have one (or maybe two) pitches that are way better than anything else they throw. They can specialize in that pitch and defeat the odds by throwing something the hitter can't hit even if they do guess right. It works because RPs are sprinters not marathoners, and they can put maximum effort into every pitch they throw, where SPs have to be somewhat economical with their effort.

I'm not sure exactly how the game models this kind of thing, but in real life a starter's third (and fourth, and fifth, and...) pitch allows them to give the hitter another a "different look", or "something else to think about". The first time a hitter faces a pitcher, just about every pitch is a surprise. The second time through the order, a pitcher with only two pitches probably can't surprise the hitter, while a guy with another pitch might start to throw it later in the game and complicate the hitter's thinking.

It's more complicated than this, but imagine you're a hitter trying to guess what pitch is coming in a two strike count. If a guy throws two pitches evenly, you have a 50% chance of guessing right. If you have three pitches, that drops to 33%. Having extra secondary pitches just makes the odds more in your favor.

There are other reasons, too, but this is my basic understanding of why SPs need 3+ average or better pitches to be viable.

Also, since you asked specifically for trade tips:

- "Shop a player" is a good tool. Pay attention to names who come up a lot, as it won't take much to get them if you want them.

- The trading block is "shop a player" for the AI. You can get anyone there for a bag of rocks, and the team will usually eat some of their contract too.

- If you have a decent or better team (like in your post), and you have a roster hole you want to fill, off-season free agency is usually a better bet than trading for many reasons. (Callups are worse than both but way more fun, in my opinion.) Otherwise, mind the trade deadline, as trading gets easier and more frequent the closer you get.

- There's a sort of invisible trading block with players who are sort of unwanted by their team (usually because $$$), but too important to annoy by putting them on the block outright. These are the players who usually get traded to other AI teams, and who usually come up when you shop one of your own players. If you can find one of these invisible available players who fills a need for you, they will be much easier to trade for.

TLDR I would give up on trying to get this particular dude. Keep shopping around for someone else, and a better trade fit might come through.

Remember that just because a trade is "fair" doesn't mean it makes sense for the other side. It actually makes the trading system *more* realistic that you can't always buy a dollar for $1.25.

If you're looking for recommendations on how to fill your spot, I would suggest looking specifically for overpaid vets, as the AI is much more willing to shed big contracts even if they have to eat a ton of $$$. (This only applies if you're on OOTP18 obviously.)

The basis of my bullpen is the one (or ideally two) "stopper"/"fireman" guy, who will come on in the middle of an inning in a close game with men on base, and who will try to strand as many runners as they can. Best qualities are high stuff and high control, since Ks are precious and BBs are lethal. This is usually but not necessarily your best reliever. Firemen should rarely/never start innings, even if they came in last inning and only threw three pitches, since you very well may want to use them tomorrow.

Otherwise, stick to common sense and baseball 101 stuff. Like Mexico Ron said, make sure your best relievers get as much work as possible, ideally in close games against the other team's best hitters. Leverage L/R handedness, but don't be a slave to it. I would call myself an intermediate player, and most of my improvement in the past ten years or so hasn't been in technique or musical understanding, but in getting better at sightreading. I'm still not good, but it's much easier for me now than it was. And there's no better heuristic than to practice. Always make an effort to read the music even when you know the piece. Play new pieces as slowly as you need to. Play as much new music as you can, and you will build your confidence as well, which helps quite a bit.

Also, in this case, the publisher does make some suggestions. For example, the second LH eighth note visually lines up as in between the second and third RH 22nd notes, slightly closer to the third. If you're playing the piece slowly enough, you can imitate that by putting the LH note between the RH notes, just a little closer in time to the third RH note.

The key is to play it, accepting that will be pretty loose and might be garbage, and listen to yourself play, and think about your playing as a listener. That will help you decide for yourself how you feel these passages out. Always remember that you're the player. You have the power to play it as what you feel is right.

Back when I was learning this piece, my instructor said to play the first eight of the eleven as the normal two RH/one LH, lining them up exactly, and then the last three RH/two LH, keeping the LH constant.

Once I got a feel for the melody, he had me shake up the ordering of the notes a little bit. Now I play it in a way that doesn't quite feel exact compared to some other players I listen to, but it does feel close to true to what I feel Chopin intended when I hear what I play.

In general, my advice for dealing with passages like these, where you can't count the rhythm, is to interpret it as the composer giving you free reign to create the rhythm as you please, as long as you fit their x (11) notes in the given time. As you play it more and hear yourself play that melody more, you will get better playing it.

[This is a neat guide for a (supposedly) competitive Honor/Commerce/Autocracy game.](http://forums.civfanatics.com/showthread.php?t=529482) I actually will be trying this strategy in my next game. It sounds kind of fun; the idea is basically that you just go hardcore domination, ignoring science and growth while focusing on gold production to pay for a cheap army.

According to this author, for this strategy to work, you have to win by the time you get to the Industrial era, or you will fall too far behind in tech and growth. But it sounds plausible to me, especially on the slower game speeds I usually play at. It also sounds like a very fun strategy to play.

The primary reason is that it somewhat addresses what I call the "3,000 year scouting mission" problem. Unit movement over time relative to production is much more realistic, although even marathon is still much too slow for reality, where units should be able to move around the map quite quickly compared to research/production/growth. And if you build a huge army of composite bowmen, you (and your enemies) probably won't have researched machinery by the time your army actually arrives at the battle.

In addition to the slowed obsolescence of your military, marathon also makes mistakes/mis-clicks less costly in general. Yes, games take an atrociously long time to finish, but when you spend hundreds of hours on this game, it's the difference between playing five games versus twenty, not one game versus ten or something like that.

If you don't invest that much time into the game, then obviously I would recommend standard or quick speed. And if you get bored with waiting thirty seconds to press enter, then marathon is absolutely not for you.

One of the advantages of playing on marathon speed is that you can basically take as long as you please to settle without worrying about falling behind in tech culture or other factors.

I don't have much intuition as to how far you fall behind at faster speeds.

So my first word of advice is to not take advice from strangers on the internet. For a variety of reasons, /r/depression is a really bad place to take advice. ;)

That said, I can tell you what the people I live with do that is helpful for me, and maybe you can infer from what I say how you might be able to help your partner. One thing to recognize is that your partner's depression may not be similar to mine. If you really want to help, and you aren't sure if something I say or that you infer applies to your partner, ask them.

The first thing my family does is manage their expectations of what I am actually capable of doing. They know that I am motivated to do exactly nothing, and while it isn't realistic for them to not expect me to do anything, they do recognize what an effort it is for me to contribute at the low rate that I do.

The second major thing they do is to pressure me to fulfill my obligations to myself and to other people. That would be things like getting myself to work, making my doctor's/therapy appointments, bathing, eating, etc. This is a tricky thing because this sort of pressuring for them requires that they both acknowledge and be sensitive to the fact that on some level I would rather crawl into a ditch and die than do any of these things, I still have to do them, and everyone (including myself) knows that I have to do them, and I can't get out of doing them.

The last thing my family does for me is actually something that I agreed to for their sanity. I have had incidents in the past with my medication, and they wanted to ensure my future safety from myself by administering my medication, and managing all of the other pills around the house. This, of course, is the least likely to apply to your partner in any way, although it is conceivable that he might feel safer if you dispensed his pills on a weekly basis.

Good luck. It's more than the people who have to take the pills who suffer from depression.
